routes.description: Infer a transcendent divine ground from objective moral facts and obligations, while challenging whether evolutionary naturalism can preserve their authority or the reliability of the reasoning used to deny them.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that objective moral value is real, that it requires a transcendent personal ground, and that the proposed evolutionary account neither supplies normative authority nor defeats trust in that inference.

motionBridge.description: Objective evil and moral obligation make a divine moral ground the better explanation.

centralBridges.description: Moral experience tracks genuinely objective value rather than preference alone.
Objective moral value requires a transcendent standard grounded in God.
Undirected evolution cannot adequately secure confidence in truth-directed moral and rational beliefs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Basic moral convictions are epistemically stronger than the skeptical premises offered against them.
Moral disagreement concerns knowledge or application and does not by itself defeat moral objectivity.

routes.description: Explain moral experience as a human-centered evolutionary phenomenon organized around flourishing, while denying that experienced obligation establishes objective value or uniquely requires a divine ground.
routes.successCriteria: Show that evolutionary and psychological mechanisms adequately explain moral experience, distinguish that explanatory burden from proving normative truth, and expose unsupported or circular steps from moral experience to God.

motionBridge.description: Agnostic atheism can explain moral experience without accepting a divine moral ground.

centralBridges.description: Evolutionary pressures and human psychology explain why moral judgments feel compelling.
Human-centered moral judgments do not remain objective independently of valuing subjects.
Moral experience does not uniquely establish God and may be explained without divine grounding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Shared concern for flourishing permits practical moral reasoning from acknowledged assumptions.
Using divinely supplied reason to establish its divine source risks explanatory circularity.

sections.title: Moral ontology and divine grounding
sections.rationale: This section contains the principal inference from evil through objective goodness to God and the direct subjectivist challenge to that inference.

sections.title: Moral phenomenology and evolution
sections.rationale: This section tests whether deeply felt moral obligation supports objectivity or can instead arise from evolved concern for survival and flourishing.

sections.title: Evolution and rational reliability
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether an evolutionary explanation undermines confidence in reasoning itself and therefore defeats the con route.

sections.title: Intuition and explanatory burden
sections.rationale: This section compares the epistemic force of basic moral convictions with the narrower evolutionary project of explaining moral experience.

sections.title: Ambiguity and objective morality
sections.rationale: This section tests whether disagreement and ambiguous cases undermine objectivity or instead fit an evolutionary pattern centered on harm and survival.

sections.title: Competing grounds of reason
sections.rationale: This section contains the final direct exchange over whether evolution or theism better grounds trustworthy reason and whether the theistic answer is circular.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Because evil is a privation of objective good and objective good is grounded in God's nature, the existence of evil supports rather than disproves God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator expressly hands the floor to Frank immediately before an uninterrupted first-person presentation of his principal argument.

response.rationale: This is the first selected statement of the principal pro inference and has no earlier selected argumentative target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly advances the complete pro route, though the grounding premise is largely definitional.

precisionFindings.rationale: The chain from evil to good to God is explicit, but the intended scope of the divine-grounding definition is not separately defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim rests on a controversial identification of goodness with divine nature that is asserted more than independently warranted.

charity.alternative: The atheistic challenge treats evil as evidence against a good God rather than evidence for God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The alternative can accept moral language while disputing either its objectivity or its need for divine grounding.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional chain is intelligible, but its decisive bridge identifies objective goodness with God's nature without an independent argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The privation account supplies a conceptual analogy, while the divine-grounding premise receives little comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the full motion-level conclusion that evil points toward a divine moral ground.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the problem-of-evil alternative accurately but compresses non-theistic accounts of moral objectivity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span contains the complete inferential chain, its privation account, and the stated conclusion concerning evil and God.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Moral wrongness is dependent on conscious valuers, and invoking a transcendent being to preserve mind-independent morality would assume the very being the moral argument seeks to establish.
moves.attributionBasis: Frank directly addresses Alex by name, after which Alex gives a sustained first-person account before Frank resumes the exchange.

components.text: Evil presupposes an objective standard of good.
Objective goodness requires grounding in God's nature.
The existence of evil therefore supports God's existence.

response.rationale: The reply rejects mind-independent moral status and identifies circularity in introducing a transcendent valuer to establish the objectivity used to infer that valuer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive grounding inference directly, though its subject-dependence premise is defended mainly by conceptual examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move defines objectivity, distinguishes human-dependent moral predicates, and expressly conditions the possible transcendent exception.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The dependence argument is carefully framed, but the claim that moral wrongness cannot persist without human psychology remains more asserted than demonstrated.

charity.alternative: The pro route reasons from experienced moral law as an effect to a transcendent moral cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro route need not presuppose the Christian God specifically, but it does require some transcendent ground.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The subject-dependence and circularity objections form a stable route, with one compressed premise about what moral predicates require.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The consciousness-removal test is relevant conceptual support, although it does not exhaust rival realist accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the central divine-grounding bridge and supports the con account of subject-dependent morality.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately represents the transcendent-being response and identifies its intended role before challenging its circular use.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span supplies a definition of objectivity, applies it to moral wrongness, and states the circularity objection to transcendent grounding.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: The pervasive, deeply ingrained experience of moral law is an effect that should be trusted as objective and explained by a transcendent moral cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with a direct first-person rebuttal and later addresses Alex's prior recorded position before Alex answers.

components.text: Objective truth is independent of human consciousness.
Moral wrongness depends on the psychology of conscious valuers.
A transcendent moral valuer cannot establish itself without circularity.

response.rationale: The reply counters subject-dependence by appealing to the experienced pressure and depth of moral law, but it does not resolve the earlier circularity challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contests a decisive premise yet leaves the distinct circularity component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The effect-to-cause proposal is recoverable, though the move slides between ingrained appearance and objective status without a clear scope condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Deep psychological entrenchment is treated as substantial evidence of objectivity without excluding powerful non-realist explanations.

charity.alternative: The con account holds that moral convictions feel objective while remaining products of human psychology.
charity.decisiveQualification: The con position does not deny the strength of moral experience; it denies the inference from felt force to mind-independent truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reasoning from a strong moral effect to a cause is intelligible, but felt objectivity does not by itself entail actual objectivity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a pervasive phenomenon but offers limited warrant for treating its apparent objectivity as veridical.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the pro route's central objectivity bridge while leaving divine grounding less fully established.

representationalCharity.rationale: It represents the con acknowledgment of deeply ingrained moral experience, but understates the distinction between appearance and ontology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span presents moral law as an experienced effect, identifies its deeply ingrained character, and asks why its objectivity should be doubted.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Evolution can instill survival and flourishing commitments that make derivative moral rules feel objective, without making the foundational commitment objectively good.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Frank's direct question in the first person and develops the same evolutionary account attributed to Alex throughout the surrounding exchange.

components.text: Moral convictions are deeply ingrained and experienced as objective.
Their experienced force gives reason to regard them as genuinely objective.
The moral effect is best explained by a transcendent cause.

response.rationale: The move preserves the phenomenological datum while replacing transcendence with an evolutionary account and explicitly denies that consensus or felt force establishes objectivity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the decisive inference by supplying an alternative mechanism and separating derivative rules from the assumed end.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between foundational assumption and derivative rule is clear, though objective sometimes denotes conditional derivability and sometimes mind independence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evolutionary account is plausibly framed and qualified, but the genetic and psychological mechanism is sketched rather than evidenced in detail.

charity.alternative: The pro account treats the depth and universality of moral conviction as evidence that moral truths are objective.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro claim concerns actual objectivity, not merely agreement or conditionally objective means to a chosen end.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an assumed end and objectively effective means is coherent and directly explains the appearance-versus-reality gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolutionary survival pressures provide a relevant mechanism, but the move supplies no detailed evidence connecting specific pressures to the full moral experience.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the central con bridge that moral phenomenology can be explained without divine grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the pro observation that moral rules feel objective while carefully disputing the ontological conclusion drawn from it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span develops the assumed-flourishing framework, connects survival motivation to evolution, and separates widespread conviction from objectivity.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: If undirected evolution produces every belief for survival rather than truth, it undermines confidence in moral beliefs and in the naturalistic conclusions drawn from them.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn challenges Alex's evolutionary explanation directly and continues in Frank's established first-person argumentative voice until Alex responds.

components.text: Evolutionary pressures instill a drive toward survival and flourishing.
That drive explains why moral rules feel objective.
Experienced objectivity need not amount to objective moral truth.

response.rationale: The reply attacks the reliability of the evolutionary explanation and expressly states the global skeptical consequence, but does not directly defeat the appearance-versus-truth distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It targets the explanatory mechanism with a serious defeater, though it does not contact every decisive qualification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability challenge is clear, but undirected evolution is repeatedly characterized as random without distinguishing mutation, selection, and truth-conducive adaptation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a global skeptical consequence without establishing that adaptive cognitive systems are unlikely to produce generally reliable beliefs.

charity.alternative: The con route uses evolution to explain moral experience rather than to prove moral propositions true.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolution is not wholly random, and fitness-oriented cognition may still correlate substantially with truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The defeater structure is intelligible, but the inference from evolutionary origin to wholesale unreliability requires a missing probability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move poses a significant challenge but supplies no base-rate or comparative warrant showing that evolved cognition is generally untrustworthy.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks a central premise of the con evolutionary route and supports the pro reliability bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It treats undirected evolution as random in a way that omits selection and the con route's narrower explanatory burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span states the evolutionary-origin premise, extends it to all beliefs, and articulates the resulting challenge to belief reliability.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Reason must be treated as a basic practical assumption for inquiry, and evolved consciousness can explain rational capacity even if ultimate certainty about its reliability is unavailable.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker uses Alex's recurring first-person framing, concedes the existential difficulty, and is then addressed by name in the following challenge.

components.text: Undirected evolution produces beliefs without a truth-directed intelligence.
An evolutionary origin therefore defeats confidence in any belief.
The defeater applies to naturalistic and moral conclusions themselves.

response.rationale: The reply resists global skepticism by treating reason as indispensable and offers an evolutionary origin for rational capacity, but does not show why that origin is truth-conducive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the global defeater directly but supplies only a pragmatic assumption and compressed evolutionary explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates the need to assume reason from the proposed evolutionary origin of rational consciousness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that reason is indispensable and evolution can explain capacity is appropriately qualified by acknowledged uncertainty.

charity.alternative: The pro challenge argues that evolution cannot warrant trust because it selects for survival rather than truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge concerns epistemic trust, not merely whether an evolutionary causal story can be proposed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The pragmatic response avoids paralysis, but indispensability does not independently answer the pro request for a reliability ground.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evolutionary explanation is plausible but asserted briefly, and no mechanism connects adaptive cognition to reliable truth acquisition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central pro reliability bridge and protects the con explanatory route, though incompletely.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the pro argument as a challenge to naturalistic reason and concedes rather than conceals the foundational assumption.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span identifies reason as an unavoidable assumption and proposes evolved consciousness as an explanation of rational capacity.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Immediate moral obligation is a properly basic belief whose epistemic force exceeds the weaker skeptical premises used to deny objective morality.
moves.attributionBasis: Frank introduces and applies an attributed philosophical argument before directly questioning Alex, who answers immediately afterward.

components.text: Reason must be assumed as a precondition of any inquiry.
Evolution can explain the emergence of rational consciousness.
Ultimate certainty about reason's reliability is unavailable.

response.rationale: The move parallels basic trust in reason with basic moral knowledge and argues that skepticism carries weaker premises, but it does not answer the evolutionary explanation directly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It addresses foundational warrant and uncertainty while leaving the causal evolutionary component untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative epistemic claim is recoverable, though the conditions under which intuition counts as properly basic remain unstated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative argument has force, but the reliability of moral intuition and possible defeaters receive limited qualification.

charity.alternative: The con route treats moral objectivity as an appearance explained by evolved assumptions about flourishing.
charity.decisiveQualification: The con route need not deny the felt certainty of moral obligation to dispute its mind-independent truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative warrant structure is coherent, but treating moral intuition as properly basic requires criteria that are not supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited comparative formulation supports the epistemic challenge, but no independent account of reliable moral intuition is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances a necessary subsidiary defense of moral objectivity rather than the complete motion-level conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly identifies moral skepticism and subjectivism as relying on premises that compete with strong moral experience.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span presents a comparative epistemic argument and applies it directly to the strength of experienced moral obligation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The evolutionary case explains why people experience actions as right or wrong; it does not claim that science makes those actions objectively right or wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex begins with a direct first-person response and explicitly distinguishes his project from the nearby account attributed to Sam Harris.

components.text: Moral obligation is experienced with exceptional intuitive force.
That intuitive force supports objective moral truth.
Skeptical premises are weaker than the basic moral conviction.

response.rationale: The reply preserves the strong experience while diagnosing a mismatch between the pro ontological demand and the con explanatory burden, then states the narrower claim it defends.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly resolves the apparent conflict by distinguishing explanation of experience from proof of normative truth.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory and normative projects are expressly separated, with a clear denial that the former establishes the latter.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The bounded explanatory claim fits the support supplied and explicitly avoids the stronger normative conclusion.

charity.alternative: The pro route treats immediate moral conviction as evidence for objective moral truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro argument is ontological, whereas the con route expressly undertakes a phenomenological explanatory burden.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between explaining belief and establishing its truth is explicit, stable, and resolves a central burden confusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is strongly warranted, although the underlying evolutionary causal account remains only broadly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally advances the con success criterion by defining and defending its actual explanatory burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately distinguishes its own narrower project from both the pro ontological claim and a stronger scientific moral realism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span expressly separates scientific explanation of moral experience from any scientific proof that particular actions are right or wrong.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Evolutionary origins threaten the reliability of all beliefs, while disagreement or uncertainty about particular moral cases no more disproves moral objectivity than scientific disagreement disproves an objective world.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex finishes his evolutionary account and Frank immediately resumes with a two-part rebuttal in his established argumentative position.

components.text: Evolution is offered to explain moral experience rather than objective moral truth.
The narrower explanatory claim avoids deriving an ought from science.
Moral experience may vary while retaining a common evolutionary basis.

response.rationale: The reply renews the reliability objection and supplies a clear epistemology-versus-ontology analogy, but it does not defeat the con distinction between explaining experience and proving truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the evolutionary mechanism and ambiguity issue while missing the decisive limitation on the con claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The disagreement analogy is clear, though the description of evolutionary production again leaves relevant causal distinctions compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The disagreement point is well calibrated, but the renewed global reliability objection remains stronger than its supplied warrant.

charity.alternative: The con account treats patterns of moral ambiguity as evidence for an evolutionary explanation of moral experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: The con argument does not infer subjectivity merely from the existence of disagreement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemology-versus-ontology analogy is coherent, while the separate global reliability argument retains an unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The scientific-disagreement comparison appropriately rebuts a crude inference, but it only indirectly addresses the actual evolutionary pattern argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary disagreement bridge and protects objectivity without completing the divine-grounding route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly distinguishes disagreement from ontology but initially risks attributing that simpler inference to the con position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span combines the evolutionary reliability objection with an analogy separating disagreement about facts from the existence of objective facts.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Moral ambiguity does not itself prove subjectivity, but its concentration around disputed harm, life, and survival classifications supports an evolutionary explanation of moral experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly corrects the immediately preceding interpretation and restates Alex's evolutionary argument in first-person terms.

components.text: Moral disagreement alone does not establish moral subjectivity.
Uncertainty about objective facts is compatible with an objective domain.
Evolutionary origins undermine confidence in all resulting beliefs.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the legitimate disagreement distinction, corrects the attributed inference, and replaces it with a pattern-based evolutionary argument, while leaving the reliability objection unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a clear corrective reframe and answers the legitimate issue with a pattern claim, but omits the separate reliability challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly denies the crude disagreement inference and precisely limits ambiguity to corroborative evidence for an evolutionary basis.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest evidential claim matches the observed pattern offered and does not claim that ambiguity deductively proves subjectivity.

charity.alternative: The pro position distinguishes uncertainty about moral facts from the possible objectivity of the moral domain.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro analogy answers disagreement alone but not necessarily patterned disagreement tied to harm classifications.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The corrective distinction and replacement pattern argument are explicit, mutually consistent, and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The examples provide relevant pattern evidence, though the inference to evolutionary origin remains underdetermined by rival cultural explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally supports the evolutionary explanation while directly answering the subsidiary disagreement issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: It explicitly disclaims the weaker inference attributed to it and preserves the legitimate content of the pro objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span corrects the disagreement interpretation and develops a narrower pattern-based inference involving harm, survival, and disputed classifications.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: If evolution gives rise to every belief, including belief in evolution, those beliefs lack a trustworthy ground unless rational capacities are designed by a rational divine mind.
moves.attributionBasis: Frank directly addresses Alex and restates the reliability dilemma before Alex immediately offers a parity objection.

components.text: Moral ambiguity is offered only as evidence for an evolutionary explanation.
The pattern centers on harm, survival, and disputed classifications.
The argument does not infer subjectivity from disagreement alone.

response.rationale: The reply attacks the general trustworthiness of the evolutionary explanation and states a defeating consequence, but does not address the specific ambiguity pattern or its qualification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies relevant contrary material and a global defeater while making little component-level contact with the selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dilemma is recoverable, but random and undesigned are treated as equivalent without distinguishing evolutionary selection or degrees of reliability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted design-or-untrustworthiness dichotomy excludes intermediate truth-conducive evolutionary accounts without sufficient argument.

charity.alternative: The con route holds that evolution can generate rational and moral capacities capable of tracking relevant features of reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Undirected evolution need not mean that every cognitive outcome is random or wholly disconnected from truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-reference challenge is intelligible, but the binary choice between divine design and untrustworthy randomness is insufficiently supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No comparative probability or mechanism is supplied to show that evolved cognition cannot be substantially truth-conducive.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the pro reliability bridge, though it does not independently complete the moral-grounding inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: It compresses evolutionary theory into random forces and omits the con position's selection-based and limited explanatory claims.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span states the self-referential reliability challenge and contrasts undirected evolutionary cognition with designed rational capacity.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The theistic account faces a parallel circularity because it uses reason allegedly supplied by God to infer that God is the rational source that validates reason.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex begins with an explicit comparison to Frank's argument, questions the proposed difference, and continues the parity objection until Frank resumes.

components.text: Evolutionary origins allegedly undermine trust in every resulting belief.
Divine design supplies a trustworthy rational capacity.
A rational divine mind provides a non-circular ground for reason.

response.rationale: The reply maps the pro reliability demand onto the theistic explanation and explicitly argues that the proposed escape relies on the very reason whose divine validation is at issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts every decisive component and exposes a clear parity problem, though parity alone does not positively vindicate evolutionary reliability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The parity claim, its target, and the alleged circular dependence between reason and divine grounding are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The circularity concern is well supported, but the claim of full symmetry may overlook differences between causal origin and ontological grounding.

charity.alternative: The pro account argues from reliable rational effects to a rational divine cause that grounds the laws of logic.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro route presents an inference to the best ground, not a deductive proof that reason exists only because God has already been established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity objection is explicit and internally stable, although the evolutionary and theistic explanatory structures may not be identical in every respect.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dependence identified is genuine and directly supported by the exchange, but the objection does not compare the rival explanations beyond circularity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It defeats a subsidiary claimed advantage of the pro route but does not itself fully establish the con evolutionary account.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately presents the theistic claim that rational capacity derives from a rational source, while somewhat compressing its abductive form.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span constructs the parity comparison, questions the proposed theistic advantage, and identifies the alleged circular dependence.
